title: The Dative
summary: The case of the person concerned: the indirect object, and the constructions in which Lithuanian says that a thing pleases to somebody or is necessary to somebody, where English would make that somebody the subject.

rules.heading: The Dative Singular
rules.statement: The **dative** answers *kam?* (to whom? for whom?) and names the person on whose behalf or towards whom the action is done. Its endings are given below; note that the masculine **-ui** and the feminine **-ai** are the marks of the case, and that the feminine dative *-ai* is not the masculine nominative plural *-ai* of ¶53.

paradigms.caption: Nominative → dative singular
paradigms.footnote: The dative plural ends in -ams, -iams, -oms, -ėms: broliams, mamoms, katėms.

examples.gloss: I am writing to my brother.
I am giving the book to my mother.

rules.heading: The Indirect Object
rules.statement: A verb of giving, sending, saying or showing may have **two** objects: the thing, in the accusative, and the person, in the dative. English marks the person with *to* or by word order; Lithuanian marks it with the ending, and the order of the two is therefore free.

examples.gloss: I give the book to my brother.
I give my brother the book.
examples.note: the same sentence; the endings settle which is which

examples.gloss: The teacher writes a letter to the father.

rules.heading: The Dative of the Pronouns
rules.statement: The personal pronouns have their own dative forms, and they are short and very common — they must be known cold, because the constructions of ¶68 and ¶69 are built on them.

rules.heading: Liking: Patikti with the Dative
rules.statement: Lithuanian does not say "I like the book" but **the book pleases to me**. The verb is **patikti**, the person who likes stands in the **dative**, and the thing liked is the **subject**, in the nominative. It follows that the verb agrees with the thing, not with the person — and that a plural thing gives a plural verb though the person is one.

paradigms.caption: The construction compared
paradigms.footnote: Compare *mėgti* (¶39), which is built as English builds it: *aš mėgstu knygą*, with the liker as subject and the thing in the accusative. Both are correct; *patikti* is the commoner in speech.

examples.gloss: I do not like the city.

rules.heading: Needing: Reikia with the Dative
rules.statement: **Reikia** — it is necessary — is **impersonal**: it has no subject at all and never changes its form. The person who needs stands in the **dative**, and what is needed follows either in the **genitive** or as an **infinitive**. English turns the person into a subject and Lithuanian does not.
footnotes: *reikia* never takes an ending for person or number: *man reikia*, *jiems reikia*, alike.

rules.heading: Other Verbs Taking the Dative
rules.statement: A group of everyday verbs governs the dative where English would use a direct object or a preposition. **Tikti**, to suit; **skambinti**, to telephone; **padėti**, to help. With these the dative is not an indirect object but the only object there is, and using an accusative is simply wrong.

vocabulary.gloss: to please, to be liked (+ dat.)
it is necessary (+ dat. and gen. or infinitive)
vocabulary.notes: Impersonal: never changes for person or number.

drills.stem: What is the dative singular of **mama**?
drills.explanation: Feminine -a makes -ai. *mamos* is the genitive and *mamoje* the locative.
*patikti* agrees with the thing liked, which is the subject *kava*, so the third person *patinka* stands. *mėgstu* would need *aš* and an accusative, and *reikia* means "is necessary".
*reikia* is impersonal and has no subject; the needer stands in the dative and what is needed in the genitive. There is no such form as *reikiu*.

The thing given takes the accusative and the person the dative, and their order is free because the endings settle the roles. The third makes the brother a second accusative; the fourth gives *padėti* an accusative where it requires a dative (¶70).

drills.stem: **Man patinka knygos.** Why is the verb not *patinku*?
options: Because *patikti* is impersonal and never changes.
Because the subject is *knygos*, not *man* — the verb agrees with the thing liked.
Because the dative always takes a third-person verb.
drills.explanation: In this construction the thing liked is the subject and the liker stands in the dative. The verb therefore agrees with *knygos*, and the third person serves both numbers (¶57). *reikia* is the impersonal one; *patikti* has a subject.

drills.stem: Complete: **Ji ____ mamai.** (She is helping her mother.)
drills.explanation: *padėti* governs the dative, and *mamai* is already in it — no preposition is wanted. *duoti* would need something given as well.

drills.stem: In which of these does the **dative** name the person concerned?
drills.explanation: *man*, *jam* and *draugui* are datives. In the second the person is the subject in the nominative, and *Vilniuje* a locative of place.

drills.stem: *Aš mėgstu kavą* and *Man patinka kava* both render "I like coffee". What is the grammatical difference?
options: None; they are interchangeable in form as well as sense.
In the first the liker is the subject and coffee the object; in the second coffee is the subject and the liker stands in the dative.
The first is present and the second impersonal.
drills.explanation: *mėgti* is built as English builds "like"; *patikti* reverses the roles, so that the verb agrees with the coffee and would become plural if several things were liked. Both are correct and *patikti* is the commoner in speech.

options: It never changes for person or number.
The person who needs stands in the dative.
What is needed stands in the accusative.
It may be completed by an infinitive.
drills.explanation: What is needed stands in the **genitive** — *man reikia pinigų* — or is replaced by an infinitive. An accusative after *reikia* is one of the commonest errors a learner makes, because English supplies a direct object there.

drills.stem: **Aš mėgstu šią knygą.** Rewritten with *patikti*, how many words of the new sentence differ in form from the old?
drills.explanation: The sentence becomes *Man patinka ši knyga*: *aš* → *man*, *mėgstu* → *patinka*, and *šią knygą* → *ši knyga*, the object turning into the subject and losing its accusative. Every word changes, and only the number of them is asked.

drills.title: Dovana mamai
drills.passage: Šiandien mamos gimtadienis. Tomas nori nupirkti jai dovaną. Jam patinka knygos, bet mamai knygos nepatinka. Jai patinka gėlės. Tomas skambina seseriai ir klausia: „Ką pirkti mamai?“ Sesuo sako: „Jai reikia naujo puodelio.“ Tomas eina į parduotuvę ir perka mamai puodelį ir gėlių.
drills.translation: Today is mother's birthday. Tomas wants to buy her a present. He likes books, but mother does not like books. She likes flowers. Tomas telephones his sister and asks: "What should I buy for mother?" The sister says: "She needs a new cup." Tomas goes to the shop and buys mother a cup and some flowers.

questions.explanation: *Jai patinka gėlės.* The books are what Tomas likes — the passage sets the two people's tastes against each other, and the datives *jam* and *mamai* are what keep them apart.

questions.stem: Which words in the passage stand in the **dative**?
questions.explanation: *jai*, *mamai* and *seseriai* all name the person concerned. *dovaną* is the thing bought and stands in the accusative — the two objects of *nupirkti* are in different cases (¶66).

questions.stem: The sister says **Jai reikia naujo puodelio.** How many words would change form if she said instead that mother needs *new cups*?
questions.explanation: Two: *naujo puodelio* → *naujų puodelių*, the genitive plural, the adjective following its noun. *jai* and *reikia* are untouched — *reikia* never changes for anything at all (¶69), and the person needing has not altered.
